This block previously claimed "about 6 weeks" and "$0.16 per day". Both were wrong and mutually inconsistent: 6 weeks is 42 days against a 25-day figure, and $0.16 x 42 = $6.72 against an $11 bar. Overstating supply is the documented reason RSC subscribers churned, so the claim is stated at the SHORT end of the merchant's 20-30 day range. The per-day figure divides by 20, not 25, for the same reason: it is the conservative end, and it is derived from live price so it cannot drift. {%- endcomment -%}

settings.text: The base. Cold-pressed virgin coconut oil reacted with food-grade lye makes real soap, plus the glycerin that comes with it — something most commercial bars strip out and sell separately. One fat. One reaction. No synthetic detergents added to do work the soap already does.

settings.title: Naturally Lathering
settings.text: Mechanism, not foam booster. Coconut soap is naturally rich in lather because the lauric acid in cold-pressed virgin coconut oil produces a fluffy, generous lather without SLS, SLES, cocamidopropyl betaine, or any of the synthetic surfactants commercial bars use to fake the foaming experience. The lather here is the soap working — not a chemical sleight of hand.

Calming Lavender uses lavender oil. Nourishing Tea Tree uses tea tree oil. Refreshing Lemongrass uses lemongrass and tea tree oils. settings.heading: Why does this bar feel different from the soap I'm used to?
settings.row_content: Most commercial bars are sodium tallowate (rendered animal fat) plus synthetic detergents like SLS. They produce an aggressive foam and a squeaky-clean feel — that squeak is your skin barrier being stripped. A coconut-oil soap lathers fluffier, rinses cleaner, and leaves skin feeling conditioned rather than tight. The first few uses may feel unfamiliar; the skin underneath is what's adjusting.

settings.heading: How long does the bar last?
settings.row_content: A single-ingredient coconut bar is harder than tallow-based commercial bars and lasts longer in a wet shower if drained between uses. Give it a dry surface — a slatted dish or a draining tray — and it will last considerably longer. Left sitting in standing water, any soap dissolves faster. The bar itself isn't the variable; drainage is.

settings.heading: Is this bar safe for sensitive skin?
settings.row_content: We built it for sensitive skin. No SLS, no synthetic fragrance, no dyes, no parabens, no EDTA — the most common reactive ingredients in conventional bars are all absent. The Pure Unscented variation has zero essential oils for customers who react to botanicals as well. Patch-test on the inner forearm for 24 hours before full use if you've reacted to soaps before.

settings.heading: Can I use this on my face?
settings.row_content: Many customers do, particularly the Nourishing Tea Tree and Pure Unscented variations. Coconut soap is more cleansing than conditioning, so if your face runs dry, follow with a moisturizer. Avoid the eye area.

settings.heading: Why is the unscented bar still lightly scented?
settings.row_content: That's saponified coconut oil itself. Cold-pressed virgin coconut oil has a natural light scent that carries through the saponification reaction into the finished bar. We didn't add fragrance — what you're smelling is the soap. Refined coconut oil is deodorized in a lab to remove that scent, along with most of the lauric acid. We use virgin oil and accept the natural scent.

settings.heading: Why coconut oil instead of tallow or palm?
settings.row_content: Tallow (rendered beef fat) is the cheapest soap base by a wide margin, which is why most commercial bars use it. Palm oil is cheap but often unsustainably sourced. We use coconut oil because the lather is excellent without foam boosters, and it lets us make the bar with one fat instead of a blend. One ingredient on the label.

settings.heading: Does the bar contain lye?
settings.row_content: Saponification is the chemical reaction between an oil and a strong alkali — sodium hydroxide (lye) for bar soap. The lye fully reacts during saponification and is consumed in the process; no free alkali remains in the finished bar. This is true of all real soap. Synthetic detergent bars skip the reaction entirely and are technically not soap — they're solidified detergent.
